extracted.intended_audience: IP policymakers, patent office statisticians, researchers, IP professionals and analysts
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts definitions, metrics and statistical/technical standards WIPO uses to measure and report patent activity worldwide (applications, grants, families, in-force, classification, normalization and counting rules). Useful for analysts and policy makers working with patent data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent is a set of exclusive rights granted by law to applicants for inventions that are new, non-obvious and commercially applicable. A patent is valid for a limited period (generally 20 years), during which patent holders can commercially exploit their inventions on an exclusive basis. In return, applicants are obliged to disclose their inventions to the public in a manner that enables others skilled in the art to replicate the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent rights are territorial. The patent system is designed to encourage innovation by granting time-limited exclusivity in exchange for public disclosure. The typical term is ~20 years from filing; differences in national law/procedure apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: To be eligible for patent protection, an invention must be new, non-obvious (involve an inventive step) and industrially/commercially applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the fundamental legal standard applied by patent offices and international searches; national/regional interpretations and thresholds vary by jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility model (definition and standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Utility model is a special form of patent right granted for a fixed period; terms and conditions differ from normal patents (generally shorter term and less stringent patentability requirements). Also referred to as petty patents, short-term patents or innovation patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Utility model applications are reported separately from invention patents in WIPO statistics and should be treated differently when comparing patenting activity across jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintenance / Renewal (keeping IP in force)
rubrics_metrics.description: An act by the applicant to keep an IP grant/registration valid (in force), primarily by paying the required fee to the IP office of the state or jurisdiction providing protection. That fee is also known as a 'maintenance fee.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trademarks can be maintained indefinitely via renewals; patents, utility models and industrial designs are maintained only for limited years. Renewal/non-payment causes lapse; maintenance patterns affect patents-in-force statistics and average age.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pending patent application (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent application filed with a patent office for which a patent has yet to be either granted or refused, and for which the application has not been withdrawn. In jurisdictions requiring a request for examination, it may refer only to applications with a request for examination or those neither granted nor refused and not withdrawn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pending status affects time-lag in published statistics; publication and grant timelines vary across offices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resident vs Non-resident application (statistical definitions)
rubrics_metrics.description: For statistical purposes, a non-resident application is filed with an IP office in which the first named applicant is not domiciled. A resident application is filed with the IP office of the state in which the first named applicant is resident.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These categories underpin office-level data (applications received) and help separate domestic activity from international filings; some offices have very high or very low non-resident shares which influence comparability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origin (country or region) (statistical definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: The origin of an application means the country or territory of residence of the first named applicant in the application. In some cases (notably the USA) the country of origin is determined by the residence of the assignee rather than that of the applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Origin-based statistics (absolute or equivalent counts) are used to analyse applicant behaviour worldwide and differ from office-based counts. Choice of origin rule affects international comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent family (definition and use)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent family is a set of interrelated patent applications filed at one or more offices to protect the same invention; applications in a family are interlinked by one or more of: priority claim, PCT national phase entry, continuation, continuation-in-part, internal priority, and addition or division.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent families are used to capture unique inventions and reduce double-counting across jurisdictions. WIPO’s family definition includes only families associated with invention patent applications (excludes utility model families). There is a time lag (up to ~3 years) in family indicators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign-oriented patent family (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent family that has at least one filing office different from the office of the applicant’s country of origin. Some foreign-oriented families may include only one filing office if the applicant files directly at a foreign office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicator of international protection strategy; used to measure geographical coverage of inventions and cross-border patenting intensity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalent application count (counting rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: For reporting data by origin, an equivalent application count accounts for regional office filings by multiplying each regional application by the number of member states (for certain organizations) or by specific counting rules: for OAPI, EAPO and GCC Patent Office multiply by number of member states; for ARIPO and EPO, count as one application abroad if applicant not resident in member state, or as one resident application and one application abroad if applicant is resident in a member state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalent counts are used to approximate the number of national-level filings represented by regional office applications and are essential when aggregating origin-based statistics; the exact multiplication rules vary by regional office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent applications vs grants vs in-force (distinct metrics and comparability cautions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Application counts, grants and patents in force are distinct metrics: applications filed, patents granted after examination, and patents maintained (in force) by payment. Application data for a given year should not be directly compared with grant data from the same year due to procedural delays and differing examination timelines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differences in examination capacity and procedural delays across offices make cross-office comparisons of grants and grant-rates difficult; WIPO compiles examination outcome data but cautions about interpretation (e.g., 'Patents granted out of total processed applications data presented should not be interpreted as the "grant rate."').

rubrics_metrics.name: Examination outcome categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent examination outcomes reported include: granted, rejected or withdrawn (abandoned).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: WIPO collects outcome data from offices; proportions of each outcome vary widely across offices (e.g., high share of rejections at some offices). Outcome proportions depend on procedural rules, applicant behaviour and office practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent-to-GDP and patent-per-population normalization metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Resident patent applications normalized by GDP (resident applications per USD 100 billion GDP) or by population (resident applications per million population) are used to compare patenting intensity across countries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normalization reveals differences in patenting intensity that raw counts mask; rankings differ depending on whether GDP or population normalization is used. Use consistent denominators and years when comparing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent families (unique inventions) metric
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent family indicators group related filings to estimate the number of unique inventions (minimize double counting from multiple filings for same invention).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Family-based measures have a time lag (up to ~3 years) but better capture unique inventions; family size indicates geographical coverage (number of offices covered).

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographical coverage of patent families (family size metric)
rubrics_metrics.description: Size of a patent family indicates the number of offices at which a patent is filed and reflects its geographical coverage; WIPO reports shares of single-office vs multi-office families and distribution by origin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High shares of single-office families (e.g., China) indicate domestic-focused filing behaviour; other origins show more multi-office families, indicating broader protection strategies. Family-size statistics help infer internationalization of inventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patents in force (definition and measurement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents in force are granted patents that remain valid across jurisdictions because maintenance/renewal fees have been paid. WIPO reports patents in force across jurisdictions and by resident/non-resident status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patents in force depend on renewal behaviour; WIPO reports longevity metrics (e.g., % of granted patents remaining in force at least 9 years after filing, % lasting full 20-year term) and average age by office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent term and lapse behaviour
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent rights generally last for up to 20 years from filing; a holder must pay maintenance/renewal fees to keep a patent valid and may let a patent lapse before full term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: WIPO reports statistics on how long patents are maintained (e.g., ~39.3% remain for at least 9 years; ~17.8% last full 20 years) and variation across offices affects patent-in-force profiles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technology field classification (IPC-based mapping)
rubrics_metrics.description: WIPO classifies patent applications by fields of technology using International Patent Classification (IPC) symbols mapped to technology fields (e.g., computer technology, electrical machinery, medical technology).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IPC-to-field mappings are not always clear-cut; IPC-based definitions are likely to capture the vast majority of related patents but may miss or misclassify edge cases. WIPO publishes IPC symbol lists (see annexes) for specific fields (e.g., energy technologies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Energy-related technology IPC definitions (annex mapping)
rubrics_metrics.description: Annex A provides IPC symbol lists used to define solar, fuel cell, wind, geothermal and hydro energy technologies for counting patents in these subfields.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IPC lists in the annex are intended to capture the vast majority of related patents, but correspondence between IPC symbols and technology fields is not always precise; use annex lists for consistent reproducible counts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting abroad filings and equivalent abroad filings
rubrics_metrics.description: WIPO reports 'patent applications filed abroad' (abroad filings) by origin and also reports equivalent counts, which adjust regional filings into equivalent national counts (see equivalent application count rules).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abroad filing metrics indicate internationalization of applicants; equivalent counts are necessary to compare origins fairly when regional office filings are involved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caveat on cross-office comparisons (procedural differences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Differences in the numbers of patents granted among offices depend on factors such as examination capacity and procedural delays; application data for a given year should not be compared with grant data from the same year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When comparing offices, account for differences in examination procedures, publication delays, treatment of utility models, and office-specific counting rules; use normalized and family-based indicators where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication date (prior art effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: Publication date is the date on which an IP application is disclosed to the public; on that date, the subject matter of the application becomes prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publication timing influences novelty/prior art status for subsequent filings and affects patent landscape analyses; publication delays vary across jurisdictions.
